claim: An emergency-locking retractor locks on either of two triggers: the car's own acceleration, or the webbing moving out of it
source_quote: activated by vehicle acceleration, webbing movement relative to the vehicle, or other automatic action during an emergency
note: FMVSS 209 S3 definition. The film's two sensors.

claim: It locks only on a sudden stop of the car or a fast pull of the belt, so in normal use the belt moves freely (the comfort reason it exists)
source_quote: locks only in response to the rapid deceleration of the vehicle or rapid spooling out of the seat belt webbing from the retractor, and increases the comfort of the seat belt assembly
note: Federal Register 2011, FMVSS 208 rulemaking, fn 3.

claim: The belt sensor: a heavy disc on the reel lags behind when the belt is pulled fast, and that lag swings a small arm into teeth that stop the reel
source_quote: upon rapid rotation of the reel due to webbing extension in an emergency, the inertia member lags behind the cam disc and so acts on the first end of the sensor arm
note: US 4,485,986. One design among several (also P98's inertial disc); the film draws it as an illustration of the principle, labelled.

claim: The car sensor: a weight (a pendulum, or a ball on a cone) that moves when the car brakes hard and pushes a pawl into the reel's teeth
source_quote: A vehicle sensor mechanism includes a pawl capable of engaging the ratchet wheel in the event of excessive vehicle acceleration. … a weight suspended in a pendulum fashion, and a ball rollable on a conical surface.

claim: The reel is spring-loaded to wind the belt back, gently: the US standard caps that pull at 7 newtons for a lap-and-shoulder belt
source_quote: Exert a retractive force of not less than 1 N and not more than 7 N when attached to a strap or webbing that restrains both the upper torso and the pelvis
note: FMVSS 209 S4.3(j)(2)(i)(A); spring: P86 'sprung in a direction of webbing retraction'.

claim: US rule: a retractor that senses the car must lock before 25 mm of belt comes out when the car decelerates at 0.7 g
source_quote: Shall lock before the webbing payout exceeds the maximum limit of 25 mm when the retractor is subjected to an acceleration of 0.7 g
note: FMVSS 209 S4.3(j)(2)(ii). VO: 'less than an inch'.

claim: US rule: a retractor that senses the belt must NOT lock before 51 mm at 0.3 g or less (so ordinary movement never locks it)
source_quote: shall not lock before the webbing payout extends to the minimum limit of 51 mm when the retractor is subjected to an acceleration no greater than 0.3 g
note: FMVSS 209 S4.3(j)(2)(iii).

claim: US rule: the car sensor must not lock when tilted 15 degrees or less, and must lock when tilted beyond 45 degrees (the test is called gravitational locking)
source_quote: not lock when the retractor is rotated in any direction to any angle of 15 degrees or less … lock when tilted at any angle greater than 45 degrees
note: FMVSS 209 S4.3(j)(2)(i)(D),(E); S5.2(j)(2)(ii) 'Gravitational locking'. Rollover is the obvious case; VO says 'if the car tips far over' and never claims the rule's purpose beyond its text.

claim: Many belts have a second mode: pull it all the way out, let it wind back, and it locks for a child seat
source_quote: converted from an ELR to an ALR by slowly pulling all of the webbing out of the retractor and then letting the retractor wind the webbing back up. In the ALR mode, the seat belt is lockable
note: Federal Register 2011. 'commonly use a switchable seat belt retractor'. The viewer's 'why does my seatbelt keep locking'.

claim: The lock itself is mechanical (inertia sensors and a pawl); the electronic part is the pretensioner, fired by the airbag crash sensors to pull slack out almost instantly
source_quote: Pretensioners are typically pyrotechnic devices but some are electro-mechanical. They are triggered by the same crash sensors that are used to determine the need to deploy the vehicle's air bags.
note: Mechanical lock: P86 (no electrical element in the locking path). VO: 'the lock has no chip'; the pretensioner is named as the electronic part. Some newer retractors add electric motors: VO never says 'no seatbelt has electronics'.

claim: A load limiter lets the locked belt give way above a set force, so it does not concentrate too much force on the chest
source_quote: load limiters allow the belt to give or yield while controlling the tension in the belt, typically by spooling it out of the retractor, to avoid concentrating too much force on the occupant's chest
note: Also N03 'preventing the shoulder belt from directing too much energy on the chest'.

claim: One common load limiter is a steel torsion bar inside the reel: it holds in small crashes, and twists at its design limit so belt spools out
source_quote: when the force applied by the webbing reaches the design limit, the torsion bar twists and allows the webbing to spool out of the retractor
note: Others: tear stitching, tearing metal (N03, N13).

claim: Renault fitted a 6 kN shoulder-belt limiter from 1995, then cut it to 4 kN in 1998 with a specially designed airbag
source_quote: the belt load limiter was a steel component designed to shear at a given shoulder force, namely 6 kN … The threshold was decreased to 4 kN and this lower belt belt-force limiter has been combined with a specially designed airbag
note: Stapp Car Crash J 45 (2001) 205-224; peer-reviewed. 'since 1995' in the same abstract.

claim: In 347 real crashes (35-75 km/h equivalent speed), the 4 kN limiter cut serious chest injuries (AIS 3+) by 75-85%
source_quote: 50 to 60% reduction for AIS 2+ was observed, as well as 75 to 85% for AIS 3+
note: Compared with belts with no limiter (pretensioners only). The 4 kN group was combined with an airbag: the VO says 'with an airbag'.

claim: Older occupants very often suffer severe chest injuries from a conventional belt in severe frontal crashes
source_quote: the oldest occupants very often sustain severe thoracic injuries due to the conventional seat belt
note: Stapp 2001 abstract.

claim: The cost: a belt that gives way lets you travel further; NHTSA notes tall or heavy occupants might spool out too far and hit the car's interior (data only lean that way)
source_quote: not tall or heavy occupants (who might spool out the belt too far and contact interior components); the analysis results lean slightly, but not yet convincingly, in those directions
note: Said as a concern, never as a proven effect: VO 'engineers worry'.

claim: By model year 2008 every new car and light truck sold in the US had pretensioners and load limiters in the front seats
source_quote: By model year 2008, all new cars and LTVs sold in the United States were equipped with pretensioners and load limiters at the driver's and right-front passenger's seats
note: Possible line in the truce.

claim: With a pretensioner and load limiter, a belted front occupant in a car has an estimated 12.8% lower fatality risk than with neither
source_quote: an estimated 12.8 percent lower fatality risk if the belt is equipped with a pretensioner and a load limiter than if it is not equipped with either (95% confidence bounds: 2.6% to 23.0%)
note: Passenger cars, CUVs, minivans; not significant yet for truck-based LTVs. Number budget: HUD only if used.

claim: MODEL: 0.7 g is a hard stop: from 50 km/h it stops a car in about 2 seconds and 14 meters
source_quote: subjected to an acceleration of 0.7 g
note: DERIVED in research/model.py (v^2/2a). HUD label MODEL.

claim: MODEL: 4 kN is the weight of about 400 kg, about five adults
source_quote: The threshold was decreased to 4 kN
note: DERIVED in research/model.py (4000 N / g = 408 kg; /80 kg = 5.1). VO 'about the weight of five adults'.
